You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: 🚀 AI Double Summit Hits Tonight! White House Hosts, OpenAI Ships: Who Gets Paid First? 12 Beneficiaries + Trading Playbook

TEXT:
🔥 US Stock Radar is live! 3 core themes + 6 selected names + 7-event calendar — where are this week’s US market setups? Tap the link for 22 trade ideas in one chart →
I. Market Backdrop: Rates Are Pressing Valuations; the Twin Summits Are the New Catalyst
US stocks pulled back Monday under rate pressure. The S&P 500 fell 0.8% to 7,683.69, and the Nasdaq dropped 0.9% to 26,820.38. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.23%, its highest since 2007. Uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz kept oil and the discount rate elevated.
Most Magnificent Seven names closed lower ( META down nearly 5%). Nvidia was the exception, up almost 2%, after the board added $150 billion to its buyback authorization, lifting the total to $235 billion — a liquidity backstop in a high-rate tape.
Attention has now shifted to two overlapping events today: White House policy signaling + OpenAI product delivery.
II. Event Breakdown: Policy on One Side, Product on the Other
1. White House meeting (policy line)
Trump and House Speaker Johnson are meeting Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Alex Karp, Dario Amodei, Greg Brockman and other tech leaders in the East Room.
Core move: launch America.gov, an AI-powered federal portal that folds scattered government services into one front door.
Policy signal: no pause on AI development, no heavy-handed regulation, and a push to balance innovation with safety so the US does not hand the race to China. If the tone stays loose, Washington flips from spectator to mega-customer — supportive for compute spend and government/enterprise software.
2. OpenAI DevDay (product line)
Altman keynotes at 10:00 a.m. PT (1:00 a.m. Wednesday, Beijing time).
Expected drops: a preview of GPT -6 Cyber (the fourth security-specialized model, limited to verified Daybreak Red teams); “nonstop” coding agents; and cyber models that scan code, find holes, and validate patches.
Commercial logic: AI moves from writing copy to writing code, finding vulnerabilities, and shipping fixes. Token burn and the value of being embedded in security platforms both get repriced.
III. Beneficiary List: Ranked by Who Gets Paid First
We think stacking names by “who gets paid first” is cleaner than stacking them by hype.
Front row: compute base (highest visibility)
Nvidia ( NVDA ): White House guest + oversized buyback + Open Agent Safety Platform.
AMD / Broadcom ( AVGO ) / TSMC ( TSM ): same training-and-inference expansion wave.
Second row: cloud and distribution (the enterprise on-ramp)
Microsoft ( MSFT ): OpenAI’s deepest cloud and distribution partner. Most DevDay enterprise rollout still runs through Azure.
Google ( GOOGL ) / Amazon ( AMZN ): backup for government cloud and in-house chips.
Third row: government applications (the most direct policy buyer)
Palantir ( PLTR ): CEO Karp is at the White House meeting. America.gov’s “one AI front door” story maps closely onto Gotham/ AIP .
Fourth row: cybersecurity (the underpriced increment)
CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) / Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) / Cisco ( CSCO ): already Daybreak partners. If GPT-6 Cyber becomes a deployable product, these platforms get it into existing SOC workflows first.
High-beta line: Musk ecosystem
Tesla ( TSLA ) / xAI-linked names: big narrative torque, equally noisy.
Core trade: today is not about picking a new theme. It is about validating the one already on the table. If the White House stresses that “government will use AI too,” and DevDay makes the Cyber + coding-agent path concrete, the tape can rotate from valuation pressure back to orders and products.
That argues for thematic exposure around the core names (NVDA, MSFT, PLTR, CRWD), not a full-size all-in. Watch the flip side: if Washington suddenly leans into safety red lines, or DevDay is demo-only with no deployment path, rich AI multiples can sell the news.
Risk note: the 10-year is still above 5.2%, and PCE plus jobs data are still on this week’s calendar. Trade carefully.
